items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I was living very near the hall with a very nice German couple. The woman's husband had disappeared during the war, and she did not know if he was alive or dead. Her name was Zimmermann, and she was living with a man named Karl...

ctx.x: Herman sat on left end of the bandstand, and the manager started giving him messages to give to me. It would not have bothered me had I not known that the manager could speak and understand some English or French. I felt that my business with whoever was in charge of the place was between he and I, and not with my men. So I told this man not to tell Herman or any one else on the band to tell me what he wished from me, and if it concerned something special, I could always bring Lily to his office, and she would…

When I had spent some days in Hamburg with the Edouard's band which was in 1949, and the first time I had ever been in Germany, a big part of the city was in ruin. When I returned this time, it was a new city and the only places I remembered was the concert hall where I had played in '49, and the director said that he would never let the place again for jazz concerts because people in the balconies were patting their feet so hard that he thought the building would cave in. I was living very near the hall with a…

The other places I remembered was the night spots in a district called St. Pauli, but better known as the Ripperbahn. As these places stayed open until the wee hours every morning and I finished at 1'30a.m. I had taken Lily to a few of the places. Claude Dunson was playing in a big German band in one of these joints. One of the places featured women wrestlers in a ring filled with mud. That was really an attraction but quite an ugly sight too.
